title: The resurrection of the body
hook: the Creed ends with the body raised
tomorrow: so what is heaven like, if Paul says no eye has seen it?

segments.voice: Yesterday: praying for the dead, and the line not broken. Maccabees gave the reason they prayed: they hoped the dead would rise. So, the body.
screen: `NOT BROKEN.` → `THEY HOPED THE DEAD WOULD RISE.`

segments.voice: Bodies are all over your feed: the glow-up, the workout split, the skincare shelf. Then at a funeral someone says the body was just a shell; the real person is gone somewhere else. The Creed takes a third road. The Apostles' Creed ends: I believe in the resurrection of the body, and life everlasting. Not the soul's escape. The body. And Luke adds a strange detail. The risen Jesus asks his friends for something to eat, and they hand him a piece of broiled fish. Why tell us about the fish?
screen: `THE FEED, OR JUST A SHELL?` → `THE CREED'S LAST LINES.` → `WHY THE FISH?`

segments.voice: Luke's answer is in the verse before. The disciples think they're seeing a ghost. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "See my hands and feet, that it is I myself; handle, and see: for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as you see me to have." Then he eats in front of them. The fish is the proof. Whatever rising from the dead is, it isn't floating free of a body. Now a second puzzle. Paul says the dead are raised with a spiritual body. Isn't that a contradiction? Paul answers with a garden. You plant a bare seed, and what comes up isn't the seed, but it isn't something else either. "It is sown a natural body, it shall rise a spiritual body." The same you, changed, no longer able to die. Paul even lists the changes: sown in weakness, it rises in power; sown without honor, it rises in glory. That's why Catholics treat the bodies of the dead with such care. Here's one to tell a friend: the Creed doesn't end with your soul going up. It ends with your body getting up. The hands you have now are part of the promise.
screen: `NOT A GHOST: FLESH AND BONES.` · `HE EATS THE FISH.` · `A SEED, SOWN AND RAISED.` · `THE SAME YOU, CHANGED.` · then, large: `THESE HANDS.`

segments.voice: Look at your hands, palms up, then turned over, slowly, as if you'd never seen them before. Every scar, every knuckle, the calluses from whatever you do. Stay with them until the bell, and if you pray, you can thank God for them as they are.
The resurrection of the body. The Creed's last promise: not escape from the body, but the body raised, changed and alive.
screen: `THE RESURRECTION OF THE BODY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Keep this one: these hands, the same you, raised and not swapped out. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1724 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SO WHAT IS HEAVEN LIKE, IF PAUL SAYS NO EYE HAS SEEN IT?`

fork.setup: your little brother asks if grandpa will need his glasses after the resurrection. what answer fits the Creed and Paul's seed?

grandpa won't have a body at all, only a soul floating free.

fork.reveal: the Creed promises the body raised, and Paul says changed: the same person, no longer able to die. the glasses are anyone's guess.

original.note: Greek: resurrection, a standing up again. the New Testament's word for rising from the dead.

what a scholar hears: Paul's Greek sōma pneumatikon, 'spiritual body' (1 Corinthians 15:44): some readers hear a body made wholly alive by the Spirit, not a body made of spirit.
guess: the dead raised bodily, changed, at the end of time
the soul leaving the body behind for good at death

chat.says: mia says her grandpa's body was just a shell, the real him is gone. is that what we believe?
options: Not quite. Catholics say the body matters and will be raised, changed, like a seed.
Basically yes. The soul's the real person; the body was only a container.
No. We believe he'll come back exactly as he was, same age, same aches.
chat.meaning: Luke's risen Jesus eats fish to show he's no ghost, and Paul says the body is sown and raised changed. The body is part of the promise.
